title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 7: Noynoy's Most Vexing Problem
keywords: beyond the reach of our laws
the Court's reversal of the midnight-appointments ban
primary_topics: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6) -- CJP's May 23, 2010 Inquirer column on the 'most vexing problem' awaiting Noynoy Aquino: the prosecution of grafters, the heart of his 'Kung walang corrupt, walang mahirap' mantra and his pledge to pursue the Arroyos' alleged ill-gotten wealth

Why Noynoy faces 'more daunting odds than his mother did' -- unlike Cory's year of 'revolutionary rule' free of 'legal niceties,' he must work within 'the gridlocks of democracy' against constitutional bodies (the Supreme Court and Ombudsman) whose members GMA 'carefully selected'

The early confrontation -- Noynoy's refusal to be sworn in by the GMA-appointed Chief Justice Renato Corona, whose 'coronation' followed the Court's reversal of 'half a century of jurisprudence banning midnight appointments' -- signaling how his crusade could 'grind to a halt' without a cooperative Ombudsman and an unbiased judiciary

The comparative lessons -- FDR's court-packing defeat (salvaged by Justice Owen Roberts's switch) and Lula's pragmatic moderation that lifted Brazil into the BRIC -- and the counsel that Noynoy must 'seize the momentum' of his 100-day honeymoon and use his People Power capital to win over the predecessor's appointees
sub_topics: Great expectations: the overwhelming mandate means the people 'expect Noynoy to solve their gnawing problems' -- to 'cleanse the cesspools of corruption, poverty, ignorance, criminality, and separatism' with 'immediate action, from Day One'

The vexing core: among many tasks (exemplary appointees, a wider congressional base, police/military reform, better tax collection, education and health), 'the most vexing problem is the prosecution of grafters' -- his 'Kung walang corrupt, walang mahirap' mantra and his pledge to investigate 'the alleged excesses and ill-gotten wealth of the Arroyos,' which is 'easier said than done'

Cory's harder-won precedent: Cory had 'one year of revolutionary rule -- undeterred by legal niceties' -- to 'dismantle the Marcos machine,' name a new Court and change the Constitution, plus five more years, 'yet these were not enough,' as 'the chase for the... Marcos wealth has not ended'

Noynoy's steeper odds: he 'would not enjoy that one year of free rule' and must immediately face 'the gridlocks of democracy and the many constitutional checks that could be misused... to stymie his reforms,' since GMA 'carefully selected all the members of the Supreme Court and the Office of the Ombudsman' -- so that, by public perception, 'she and her cronies would be beyond the reach of our laws'

The Corona flashpoint: Noynoy had criticized GMA's appointment of Chief Justice Renato Corona and vowed to 'break tradition and refuse to be sworn in by the new chief magistrate' -- an 'early confrontation... symptomatic of the difficulties he would be facing'

Why cooperation is indispensable: his anti-corruption drive 'would surely flounder' against a hostile Court (which had 'reversed half a century of jurisprudence banning midnight appointments to usher the coronation of its new chief'), and any commission to probe the Arroyos 'would amount to nothing without a cooperative Ombudsman and an unbiased judiciary' -- bodies armed with 'fixed terms' and 'fiscal and administrative independence'

The FDR lesson: Franklin Roosevelt, given an 'enormous mandate' amid the Depression, saw 'much of his New Deal' struck down and tried to 'pack' the Court -- a proposal 'defeated' amid protests, though he 'prevailed anyway' when Justice Owen Roberts 'switched positions' to create a sympathetic majority

The Lula lesson and the counsel: Brazil's Lula da Silva, after 'moderating his ideas,' used his capital to lift Brazil into 'BRIC' and earned Obama's G20 praise as 'the most popular politician on earth' -- so Noynoy, given the media's '100 days of honeymoon,' must 'immediately seize the momentum' and use his People Power capital to win over the constitutional structures 'dominated by appointees of the predecessor'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 7 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's May 23, 2010 Inquirer column, identifies the 'most vexing problem' awaiting Noynoy Aquino: the prosecution of grafters -- the heart of his 'Kung walang corrupt, walang mahirap' mantra and his pledge to pursue 'the alleged excesses and ill-gotten wealth of the Arroyos' -- which is 'easier said than done.' Cory, he recalls, had 'one year of revolutionary rule -- undeterred by legal niceties' to 'dismantle the Marcos machine,' name a new Court and change the Constitution, plus five more years, 'yet these were not enough,' since 'the chase for the... Marcos wealth has not ended.' Noynoy faces 'more daunting odds': he 'would not enjoy that one year of free rule' and must immediately confront 'the gridlocks of democracy and the many constitutional checks that could be misused... to stymie his reforms,' because GMA 'carefully selected all the members of the Supreme Court and the Office of the Ombudsman' -- so, by public perception, 'she and her cronies would be beyond the reach of our laws.' The early flashpoint was Noynoy's vow to 'refuse to be sworn in' by GMA's new Chief Justice Renato Corona, whose appointment followed the Court's reversal of 'half a century of jurisprudence banning midnight appointments' -- a sign that his crusade 'would surely flounder' without 'a cooperative Ombudsman and an unbiased judiciary,' bodies armed with 'fixed terms' and independence. CJP draws two comparative lessons: Franklin Roosevelt, his New Deal gutted by the US Supreme Court, tried to 'pack' it and lost, yet 'prevailed anyway' when Justice Owen Roberts 'switched positions'; and Brazil's Lula, after 'moderating his ideas,' lifted his country into 'BRIC' and earned Obama's G20 praise as 'the most popular politician on earth.' His counsel: with the media's '100 days of honeymoon,' Noynoy must 'seize the momentum' and use his People Power capital -- not 'frontal criticisms' -- to win over the constitutional structures still 'dominated by appointees of the predecessor.'
